passage.title: 安全帽的百年演變（The Evolution of the Hard Hat）
passage.text:
A hard hat is a helmet worn mainly at worksites to protect the head from injuries caused by falling objects. __31__

The hard hat was invented in 1919 by Edward W. Bullard, who had just returned from World War I. Before the war, workers used to smear their hats with tar to protect their heads. __32__ The result was the Hard Boiled Hat, which was cheap enough for every worker and light enough to wear all day long. Made of steamed canvas and glue, with a leather brim and a coat of black paint, it also had a suspension system inside to soften blows. Hard hats soon came into wide use, and they were later required on major construction projects such as the Hoover Dam in 1931 and the Golden Gate Bridge in 1933.

Over the past century, hard hats have improved considerably, moving from canvas and leather to aluminum, fiberglass, and, eventually, thermoplastic. __33__ A ventilated hard hat, for example, keeps its wearer cooler, while a see-through face shield protects the face without blocking the view. Today, available attachments include radios, sensors, cameras, and much more.

__34__ Yellow is usually worn by general laborers and contractors, white (or sometimes black) by supervisors and managers, and green by inspectors and new workers. No law sets these colors, though, so they can vary from company to company and site to site.

New products continue to expand the market for hard hats. Yet from Bullard’s canvas hat to today’s models fitted with sensors and cameras, the hard hat’s main job has never changed: keeping workers’ heads safe.

passage.title: 西尼羅病毒流行的原因（Why West Nile Spreads）
passage.text:
West Nile is a viral disease that begins in birds, which pass it on to mosquitoes that then go on to infect human beings with a bite. Most people who contract West Nile never develop any symptoms. In those who do, symptoms appear 2 to 14 days after the bite. About one in five infected people develops a fever, headaches, and body aches, usually lasting a week or so. A far less lucky one in 150 suffers high fever, tremors, paralysis, and coma. __31__

That is what made the major outbreaks of West Nile in the U.S. in the summer of 2012 so frightening. The situation was particularly bad in and around Dallas, Texas, where the virus sickened nearly 400 people and killed 19 that year. __32__ Some residents objected, fearing that the cure could be worse than the disease.

Why was the summer of 2012 so hospitable to the West Nile virus and the mosquitoes that carry it? __33__ An extremely mild winter allowed more mosquitoes than usual to survive. The unusually high temperatures of the scorching summer that followed increased their numbers further by speeding up their life cycle. The economic crisis may also have played a role. Homeowners who could not pay their bank loans were forced to abandon their houses, sometimes leaving behind swimming pools that became excellent mosquito breeding grounds.

__34__ Dallas County was not doing some of the key things that help slow the spread of West Nile, such as testing dead birds for the virus and setting out enough mosquito traps. Diseases like West Nile thus have as much to do with what officials fail to do as with climate.

passage.title: 茶在英國普及的經過（How Tea Spread Through Britain）
passage.text:
Tea is now the most typical English drink, but it took about two hundred years to reach every home in Britain. Much of its early popularity came from a foreign princess, Catherine of Braganza, who married King Charles II in 1662. __31__

The fashion soon spread beyond the circle of the nobility to the middle classes. In London, tea became a popular drink at the coffeehouses, where people met to do business and discuss the news. __32__ It came with a high price tag, and the government taxed it heavily as well. Many workers drank it only at work, where employers served them a cup in midmorning, creating a lasting British custom, the “tea break.”

__33__ At the time, the rich usually ate nothing between lunch and dinner, which might not be served until eight o’clock. The Duchess of Bedford is often said to have started the custom by having tea with bread, butter, and cake at about four o’clock. Thin sandwiches, named after the eighteenth-century Earl of Sandwich, were soon added to the menu.

As tea became much cheaper during the nineteenth century, it finally spread to every corner of British society. __34__ Unlike the light afternoon tea of the rich, this filling evening meal came to be called “high tea.” Today, people in Britain drink tea at any time of the day, whether they are rich or poor.

passage.title: 引水人的專業（The Expertise of Marine Pilots）
passage.text:
Ships are the lifeline of trade among countries. Almost everything, from food to machinery, comes by way of the sea in huge ships commanded by captains. But a ship’s captain usually guides the vessel only until it reaches the waters just outside a port, where it waits to enter the harbor. __31__

A marine pilot, often a former ship captain, is an expert with specialized knowledge of a particular port or harbor. The pilot is needed to direct large ships into a port, where deep channels are often surrounded by shallow seabeds. __32__ Both the ship and its cargo could then be badly damaged, and some kinds of cargo might be dangerous if released into the sea.

In addition to shallow seabeds, tide and wind pose further challenges for bringing ships into a port. __33__ The same strategy for docking a vessel during an incoming tide may not work during an outgoing tide. Also, the wind can significantly alter the direction of the ship and how it reacts, adding to the difficulty of docking it.

__34__ Above all, it is about risk management. A marine pilot goes on board at a crucial time and directs the vessel based on his or her knowledge of the port and the situation at hand. The pilot is responsible for not only the safety of the ship but also the protection of the port and the marine environment.

passage.title: 引水人的專業（The Expertise of Marine Pilots）
passage.text:
Ships are the lifeline of trade among countries. Almost everything, from food to machinery, comes by way of the sea in huge ships commanded by captains. But a ship’s captain usually guides the vessel only until it reaches the waters just outside a port, where it waits to enter the harbor. __31__

A marine pilot, often a former ship captain, is an expert with specialized knowledge of a particular port or harbor. The pilot is needed to direct large ships into a port, where deep channels are often surrounded by shallow seabeds. __32__ Both the ship and its cargo could then be badly damaged, and some kinds of cargo might be dangerous if released into the sea.

In addition to shallow seabeds, tide and wind pose further challenges for bringing ships into a port. __33__ The same strategy for docking a vessel during an incoming tide may not work during an outgoing tide. Also, the wind can significantly alter the direction of the ship and how it reacts, adding to the difficulty of docking it.

__34__ Above all, it is about risk management. A marine pilot goes on board at a crucial time and directs the vessel based on his or her knowledge of the port and the situation at hand. The pilot is responsible for not only the safety of the ship but also the protection of the port and the marine environment.

passage.title: 大象怎麼分辨敵友（How Elephants Spot Their Enemies）
passage.text:
Most of us find it easy to tell our friends from our enemies. But can other animals tell which humans pose a threat to them, and if so, how? __31__

In Kenya, researchers studied how elephants respond to men from two local ethnic groups, the Maasai and the Kamba. The Maasai raise cattle, and their young men sometimes spear elephants to prove their manhood. The Kamba are mainly farmers and pose little danger to the animals.

__32__ The researchers placed clothing near groups of elephants; some pieces were clean, while others had been worn for five days by a Maasai or a Kamba man. When the elephants smelled clothing worn by a Maasai man, they moved away faster and farther than they did from the other pieces. They also took longer to relax afterward and headed for tall grass. Because they never came close enough to see the clothing, its scent was the only clue they had.

__33__ In the same study, the elephants were shown clean red and white clothing. They behaved far more aggressively toward the red pieces than toward the white ones. Red is the color young Maasai men typically wear.

The researchers believe that the elephants react differently because they interpret smells and sights in different ways. Smelling a potential danger means that a threat is nearby, so the best thing to do is run away and hide. __34__ Therefore, instead of showing fear and running away, the elephants express their anger and become aggressive.

options.B: Some deep-sea squid even release a cloud of glowing liquid to confuse an approaching predator.
options.C: On land as in the sea, living lights can be used to deceive other animals.

passage.title: 動物發光的用途（What Living Lights Are For）
passage.text:
Some animals have organs in their bodies that produce light. Most of them live in the sea, but some live on land. When it is dark, they flash their lights on and off for a number of reasons. __31__

Some fish produce light in the blackness of the sea. When night falls over the Red Sea, tiny flashlight fish swim up from deep water to feed, each with a pair of “headlamps,” one beneath each eye. The light comes from bacteria that live inside the headlamps and glow all the time. __32__ By blinking their lights, the fish communicate with one another, and a fish guarding its home area blinks faster when an intruder comes near. When a predator approaches, a flashlight fish swims slowly in one direction with its lights on, then blinks them off and darts away in another direction.

__33__ After darkness falls in some parts of North America, female fireflies wait in the grass. The males fly overhead, flashing light from the undersides of their bodies. As there are many species of firefly, the males of each kind flash their own particular signal. Recognizing the flashing code of her own species, a female flashes back to one of the males, and he lands beside her.

__34__ When they are hungry, some female fireflies lure the males of other species to them. They flash a false reply when these males signal overhead, but eat the males as soon as they land. Eating the males also gives the females chemicals that protect them from spiders.

passage.title: 剛果的霍加狓（The Okapi of Congo）
passage.text:
The okapi is a mammal living in one of the most biodiverse areas of central Africa. The animal was little known to the Western world until the early 20th century, and it is often described as half-zebra, half-giraffe, as if it were a mixed-breed creature from a Greek legend. __31__ The okapi is to the country what the giant panda is to China or the kangaroo to Australia.

Although the okapi has striped markings like those of a zebra, it is most closely related to the giraffe. It has a long neck and large, flexible ears. Its face and throat are grayish white. Its coat ranges from chocolate to reddish brown, in sharp contrast with the white horizontal stripes and rings on its legs and its white ankles. __32__ The okapi is much smaller, about the size of a horse, and looks more like a deer than a giraffe. While both male and female giraffes have horns, only male okapis do.

__33__ In the years that followed, Europeans in Africa heard more stories of an animal that they came to call the “African unicorn.” Explorers may have caught only a fleeting glimpse of its striped backside as it fled into the bushes, leading to speculation that it was some sort of rainforest zebra. Some even believed that the okapi was a new species of zebra. __34__

In 1992, the Okapi Wildlife Reserve was established in northeastern Congo to protect this rare mammal. But decades of political turbulence have let many of Congo’s natural resources slip out of the government’s control, and okapi numbers have fallen by more than half since 1995. Today, perhaps only 10,000 to 15,000 remain.

passage.title: 社會連結與心臟健康（The Power of Social Connection）
passage.text:
In the 1960s and 1970s, Japanese men posed a puzzle for public health researchers. Most of them smoked, and smoking is one of the strongest risk factors for heart disease. __31__ What, then, was protecting their hearts?

Researchers in the United States and Japan set out to find the answer. They studied nearly 12,000 men of Japanese descent between the ages of 45 and 69. The men lived in Japan, Hawaii, or California, so the researchers could compare people with the same roots in three very different places. __32__

The usual risk factors, such as high blood pressure and cholesterol, explained some of the gap between the groups, but not all of it. Diet was another obvious suspect, since many of the men in America had switched from rice and fish to hamburgers and fries. Yet even the change in diet left part of the gap unexplained.

__33__ A second study of about 3,800 Japanese Americans in California found that the most traditional men had as little heart disease as men in Japan. They had been raised in Japanese culture and belonged to close-knit groups whose members supported one another. Among men who had adopted a Western way of life with looser social ties, the rate was three to five times higher.

The researchers suggested that close-knit groups may have protected the men from stress, which can harm the heart. __34__ We need to feel part of something bigger in order to thrive. And we need that sense of belonging not only online but in the real world of hugs, handshakes, and pats on the back.

passage.title: 美國烹飪節目的演變（The Evolution of American Cooking Shows）
passage.text:
American cooking programs have taught audiences, changed audiences, and changed with audiences from generation to generation. In October 1926, the United States Department of Agriculture created a fictional radio host named Aunt Sammy. Over the radio, she gave homemakers advice on all kinds of household matters, but it was mostly her recipes that caught listeners’ attention. The show helped spread cooking tips and led to a nationwide exchange of recipes.

Cooking shows moved to television in the 1940s. By the 1950s, they were often hosted by a cook who explained step by step how to prepare a dish. __31__ Poppy Cannon, for example, was the popular author of “The Can-Opener Cookbook.” She appeared on television, using canned foods to show how to cook quickly and easily.

__32__ Over time, cooking shows grew less fancy and began to feature dishes from all over the world. One well-known example is Martin Yan’s “Yan Can Cook,” which began airing on American public television in 1982. On the show, Yan taught Chinese cooking and signed off with the catchphrase “If Yan can cook, so can you!”

By the 1990s, cooking shows covered everything from elegant restaurant dishes to healthy home meals. Good food alone, however, was not enough to make a show a hit. __33__

In the early 21st century, new shows were created to please audiences who loved celebrities and reality TV. Some were filmed outside the studio, and many turned cooking into a contest between chefs. Top chefs have become as famous as rock stars. __34__ Cooking from a show’s recipes, as Aunt Sammy’s listeners once did, has gone out of style.

passage.title: 語言教室的起落（The Ups and Downs of the Language Lab）
passage.text:
One of the best-known technological aids in language teaching is the language laboratory. __31__ Students can record their own responses and play them back, while a teacher listens in and checks their progress.

When language labs first appeared, they were praised as a way to make language learning faster and more effective. They would take the burden of repetitive drills away from teachers, give learners more chances to practice listening and speaking, and let learners work at their own pace and keep track of their own progress. Many schools were quick to install the expensive equipment. __32__

There were several reasons for the language lab’s failure to live up to expectations. The recorded materials were often poorly designed, leaving students frustrated and bored. The published programs had little to do with the work students were doing in class. Few language teachers had received any training in designing materials or in running a lab. And once installed, the equipment proved difficult to maintain.

__33__ The newer labs contained much more than the traditional tape-based systems. Computer programs and video materials, in particular, proved extremely popular with learners.

__34__ For example, recordings can give learners a wide variety of natural, clearly recorded speech to help them sharpen their listening skills. Labs can also serve as resource centers, much like libraries, where learners get extra practice at a level they choose.

passage.title: 冰島的「100% Fish」計畫（Iceland’s 100% Fish Project）
passage.text:
In 2020, Petur Oddsson, a power station worker in Iceland, was struck by a 60,000-volt current. The electric shock burned almost half of his body and melted away several layers of his skin. Burns this deep and extensive can be fatal. __31__

That treatment was one result of a larger effort in Iceland called “100% Fish.” As its name suggests, the project aims to put every part of each fish caught to use. It also hopes to change the fishing industry by encouraging new uses for fish.

__32__ In Iceland, as recently as 2003, people knew how to use only about 40% of each cod they caught. The rest, about 60% of the fish, went to waste. With the help of 100% Fish, Icelanders have now found uses for almost 95% of each cod.

Nearly every part of the fish now ends up in some kind of product. __33__ Dried fish heads and spines are shipped to West Africa, where they form the base of a protein-rich soup. Omega-3 capsules, sprays that help protect against colds, and dog snacks are made from parts that were once thrown away.

Iceland’s success depends largely on people from different fields working together. The project brings fishing companies together with universities, startups, and research teams. __34__ Each cod caught in Iceland is now worth far more than it used to be. The project also offers the world a useful model for making better use of natural resources.

passage.text:

passage.title: 仙人掌外皮發電（Turning Cactus Waste into Power）
passage.text:
The prickly pear cactus is such a powerful symbol in Mexico that it occupies a prime spot on the country’s national flag. The plant was considered sacred by the ancient Aztecs, and modern-day Mexicans eat it, drink it, and even use it in medicines and shampoos. Now the bright green plant is being put to a new use: producing renewable energy.

Known locally as nopal, the prickly pear is farmed on a massive scale in Mexico. For years, only its soft, edible flesh was used. __31__

Milpa Alta, a farming district in the south of Mexico City, grows about 200,000 tons of prickly pear a year. Up to 10 tons of it ends up as waste on the floor of the local cactus market every day. __32__ Its biogas generator, set up at the market as a pilot project, turns cactus skins into gas that can be used to make electricity. Vendors there welcome this new way to use skins that once went straight into the trash.

__33__ For one thing, only the skin of the cactus is used for fuel, while the inner flesh is still eaten. Using the plant as a fuel source will therefore not push up food prices. The cactus also needs very little water, so it can grow on dry land that is unsuited to most food crops. As a result, it does not take water or farmland away from food production.

__34__ City officials would like to set up similar generators at other produce markets in the capital. If the project can be expanded in this way, the prickly pear could be the key to Mexico’s energy future.

passage.title: 用聲音驅趕鐵軌上的鹿（Sounds That Keep Deer off the Tracks）
passage.text:
Researchers in Japan have fitted a train with a speaker that barks like a dog and snorts like a deer. The unusual noises are meant to drive deer away from the tracks before the train can hit them.

On Japan’s railways, collisions with deer have become a common and serious problem. __31__ Each time, trains were stopped or delayed for at least 30 minutes.

Deer are drawn to railway lines because they need iron in their diets. They lick the rails to pick up iron filings produced as the wheels grind against the tracks. Over the years, several ways of scaring them off have been tried. __32__

The new device, developed by a team at Japan’s Railway Technical Research Institute (RTRI), relies on sound rather than sight or smell. According to RTRI researchers, deer repeatedly give short, shrill snorts to warn one another of danger. __33__ The team added the barking of a dog, an animal that deer greatly fear. When deer hear a 3-second snort followed by about 20 seconds of barking, they panic and run away from the tracks.

__34__ Encouraged by the outcome, RTRI now plans to set up fixed barking devices where deer are often seen. Officials have promised, though, that the noises will not be played in areas where people live beside the tracks.

passage.title: 海蛇怎麼喝到淡水（How Sea Snakes Get Fresh Water）
passage.text:
Many marine animals, including penguins and marine iguanas, have evolved special glands to get rid of excess salt. In penguins these glands sit just above the eyes, and marine iguanas sneeze the salt out through their noses. Sea snakes have salt glands too, under their tongues, but these glands cannot handle the massive amounts of salt that would enter their bodies if they actually drank seawater. This poses a serious problem when it comes to getting enough water to drink. If seawater is not an option, how do these snakes survive in the ocean?

For the yellow-bellied sea snake, which usually spends all of its time far from land, rain is the only source of fresh water. When it rains, a thin layer of fresh water forms on top of the ocean. __31__

An international team of researchers focused on a population of yellow-bellied sea snakes in the Pacific waters off Costa Rica, where the dry season can last six or seven months. During those dry months, the snakes presumably have nothing to drink. __32__

The researchers collected more than 500 of the snakes and weighed them. During the dry season, nearly half of the snakes drank the fresh water the team offered them, while almost none did in the wet season. __33__ Thinner, more withered snakes were more likely to drink, and they drank more. Finally, as predicted, snakes captured in the dry season contained significantly less body water than those scooped up in the wet season.

__34__ The snakes may stay dehydrated for six or seven months at a time. Scientists believe that dehydration at sea, especially during long droughts, may explain why sea snake numbers are falling in some parts of the world.

passage.title: 畢業舞會的變遷（How the Prom Has Changed）
passage.text:
The high school prom is the first formal social event for most American teenagers. It has also been a rite of passage for young Americans for about a century.

The word “prom” was first used in the 1890s for formal dances at which guests would display their fashions and dancing skills during the evening’s grand march. In the United States, parents and educators have come to regard the prom as an important lesson in social skills. __31__

The first high school proms were held in the 1920s. By the 1930s, proms had become common across the country. __32__ Prom-goers were well dressed but not fancily dressed up for the occasion: boys wore jackets and ties, and girls their Sunday dresses. Couples danced to music provided by a local amateur band or a record player. After the 1960s, and especially since the 1980s, the prom in many areas has become a serious exercise in excessive consumption, with boys renting expensive tuxedos and girls wearing designer gowns. Stretch limousines are often hired to drive prom-goers to expensive restaurants or discos for an all-night extravaganza.

__33__ Many of them worry about their self-image and about fitting in with their peers. Prom night can be a dreadful experience for socially awkward teens or for those who fail to find a date.

__34__ There have been reports, for example, of proms organized by and for homeless youth. There have also been “couple-free” proms, to which all students are welcome.

passage.title: 催眠到底是什麼（What Hypnosis Really Is）
passage.text:
When Dr. David Spiegel emerged from a three-hour shoulder surgery in 1972, he did not use any pain medication to recover. __31__ It worked—to the surprise of everyone but Spiegel himself, who has studied hypnosis for 45 years.

Hypnosis is often misunderstood as a kind of sleep in which a person does whatever he or she is told to do. __32__ When hypnotized, you tune out most of the stimuli around you. You focus intently on the subject at hand, to the near exclusion of any other thought. This trance-like state can be an effective tool to control pain, ease anxiety, and deal with stress.

__33__ In a recent study, Spiegel and his colleagues found that people who are easily hypnotized tend to be more trusting of others, more intuitive, and more likely to get caught up in a good movie. The research team compared people who were highly hypnotizable with those low in hypnotizability.

Both groups were given fMRI scans under several different conditions: at rest, while recalling a memory, and during two sessions of hypnosis. The researchers saw some interesting changes in the brain during hypnosis—but only in the highly hypnotizable group. __34__

This helps explain how hypnosis can have powerful effects, including reducing stress, anxiety, pain, and self-consciousness. Spiegel hopes that the practice can be used to replace painkillers. His own earlier research has shown that when people in pain were taught self-hypnosis, they needed half as much pain medication and suffered half as much pain as those who were only given painkillers. However, more needs to be learned about hypnosis before its full potential can be harnessed.

passage.title: 自行車的始祖（The Ancestor of the Bicycle）
passage.text:
Born in 1785 in southwestern Germany, Baron Karl Drais was one of the most creative German inventors of the 19th century. The baron’s numerous inventions include an early keyboard typewriter, the meat grinder, and a device to record piano music on paper. But it was the running machine, the ancestor of the modern bicycle, that made him famous.

The running machine, also known as the Draisine or the hobby horse, was a very primitive bicycle. With no chain or pedals, it moved only when riders pushed off the ground with their feet. The frame and wheels were made of wood. __31__ It was the first vehicle with two wheels placed one behind the other. Riders also steered it with a bar much like a modern handlebar.

__32__ Horses cost a lot to buy, and they had to be fed even when they were not being used. A muscle-powered two-wheeler, he believed, could replace them and let large numbers of people travel faster than on foot.

Drais made his first recorded ride on June 12, 1817, covering 13 kilometers in about an hour. The same trip usually took a horse-drawn mail coach four hours. The next year, Drais introduced the machine in Paris, where it quickly caught on. Riders in Britain were soon racing on their own copies of it. __33__

The success of the hobby horse was short-lived, though. The machines were heavy and difficult to ride. Safety was an issue, too, because riders often sped along the sidewalks. Collisions with unsuspecting pedestrians were frequent, and within a few years many European and American cities had banned the machine. __34__ Decades later, in the 1860s, French inventors added pedals to the front wheel and took a big step toward the modern bicycle.

passage.title: 國歌曲調的歐洲根源（The European Roots of National Anthems）
passage.text:
Over the past three hundred years, a national anthem has been one of the first things a country establishes when it gains its freedom or independence. Anthems are generally performed at formal state occasions and at other events that celebrate the nation’s identity.

passage.title: 樂高積木的五十年（Fifty Years of Lego Bricks）
passage.text:
The Lego Group had a very humble beginning in the workshop of Ole Kirk Christiansen, a carpenter from Denmark. __31__ Local families liked them so much that he decided to make toys his main business. A few years later, he named the company Lego, from the Danish words leg godt, which mean “play well.”

In 1947, the company expanded into making plastic toys, and it soon began producing early versions of its building bricks. At first, retailers and customers did not think highly of them, since most people preferred toys made of wood or metal. Many of the company’s shipments were returned after poor sales. __32__

However, Christiansen’s son, Godtfred Kirk Christiansen, saw immense potential in the plastic bricks. He believed they could become a system for creative play. __33__ In 1958, the modern interlocking brick design was finally developed and patented. Small tubes underneath each brick now gripped the one below, so a model stayed in one piece until a child pulled it apart.

__34__ A castle could be taken apart and turned into a ship, and pieces from a new set fit the ones a child already had. By 2008, Lego was sold in more than 130 countries, and about seven Lego sets were sold every second.

Fans around the world celebrated the brick’s 50th anniversary that year. Over those fifty years, the brick itself had hardly changed. A brick made in 1958 still fits one made today, and that is probably why the toy has never fallen out of favor.

passage.title: 島上哺乳類的體型變化（How Island Mammals Change Size）
passage.text:
Islands are quite different from continents and other mainland areas. The size and isolation of islands have a profound effect on island ecosystems and their inhabitants.

Scientists who study species evolution have found that mammals that settle on islands often end up a very different size from their relatives on the mainland. __31__ This pattern, first described by J. Bristol Foster in 1964, is known as Foster’s rule, or the island effect. Although there are a number of exceptions, the trend generally holds true for both fossil species and mammals living on islands today.

__32__ In a mainland environment, being large is often a safer and more adaptive way for an animal to avoid predators. On an island, with few natural predators and less competition, being large is no longer an advantage. In fact, great size can become a burden, since a huge animal needs far more food to survive and reproduce.

A study of fossil elephants from islands around the world suggests that how much big mammals shrink depends on the kind of island they live on. On balanced islands with many kinds of animals, competition with other large plant-eaters often keeps big mammals from shrinking very much. __33__

Red deer on Jersey, one of the Channel Islands about 14 miles off the coast of France, show how far and how fast big mammals can shrink. When rising seas cut the island off from the mainland, a group of normal-sized red deer was trapped there. __34__ The whole process took less than 6,000 years.

passage.title: 從刺果到魔鬼氈（From Burrs to Velcro）
passage.text:
One fine morning in 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral went for a walk in the woods with his dog. When they got home, he found a lot of burrs from a wild plant stuck to the dog’s fur and to his pants. Curious about how they held on so tightly, he rushed to his microscope to take a closer look.

To the naked eye, the tips of the burrs looked straight. Under the microscope, though, he could see that each tip actually ended in a tiny hook. The hooks had caught on the small loops of thread in his pants and clung to them firmly. __31__

Developing a real product took years of hard work. De Mestral’s first challenge was finding a material strong enough for the job. __32__ Synthetic fibers turned out to be the answer, and he finally settled on nylon. The improved fastener had about 300 hooks in every square inch, so it stayed firmly closed yet could be pulled apart easily. He named it “Velcro,” from the French words velours (velvet) and crochet (hook). By 1955, he had patented his invention, and he soon began mass-producing it in factories in Europe and later in Canada and the United States.

__33__ Because most fashion critics found it ugly and cheap-looking, it was used mostly on sports equipment such as ski gear and diving suits. Its popularity grew quickly in the 1960s, when NASA began using it to keep objects from floating around in spacecraft.

__34__ It is used on clothing and shoes, children’s toys, airplane seat cushions, blood pressure cuffs, and surgical gowns. Most impressively, it even helped hold together the first artificial heart.

passage.title: 俄羅斯飲酒習慣的由來（How Russia Took to Drinking）
passage.text:
Russia is widely portrayed as the most alcohol-dependent country in the world. Critics of the country say that drinking is almost an inherent trait of the Russian people. However, there is more to the story.

__31__ Before Russia adopted Christianity in the 10th century, people drank mostly beverages with low alcohol content. Vodka, Russia’s national drink, was not a Russian invention. It began as a strong grape spirit that visitors from Genoa, Italy, brought to Moscow in the late 14th century. Russian monks later learned to make their own version of the drink.

Records from the 15th and 16th centuries give contradictory information about how much Russians drank. Some documents noted that Russians “indulge in excessive drinking whenever the occasion arises,” while others claimed that Russians “rarely drink wine.” __32__ There were many sayings about their love of alcohol, such as “drunk as a German.”

The Russian state played a significant role in the spread of drinking. For hundreds of years, the government controlled the vodka trade and collected huge revenues from it. With so much money at stake, Russia’s rulers had every reason to keep people drinking. In the 1860s, changes in government policy caused vodka prices to drop sharply. __33__

Meanwhile, a powerful anti-alcohol movement started in the 19th century. Government policies were introduced and public organizations were set up to prevent the spread of alcoholism. __34__ Although Russia does not rank first in alcohol consumption per person, it is still among the heaviest-drinking countries in the world.

passage.title: 泰武國小古謠傳唱隊（Young Voices, Ancient Songs）
passage.text:
The Taiwu Elementary School Folk Singers are a group of Paiwan children from a small school in Pingtung, southern Taiwan. __31__ In 2009, they were invited to perform in several European countries, including Belgium, France, and Germany. Two years later, viewers of the Japanese TV program “Amazing Voice” voted them one of the world’s top five performance groups.

Recalling the group’s first tour of Europe, Camake Valaule, a physical education teacher and the group’s founder, admitted that he had felt very nervous. Most of the 75-minute show was sung a cappella, that is, without any instruments, so he had worried that the audience would fall asleep. __32__ Afterward, people told him that the performance let them picture the children’s village without ever having visited it. The experience greatly boosted the group’s confidence.

__33__ It used to be that only tribal elders in their fifties and sixties could sing these songs. Now that the children perform them, many parents have begun to ask why they themselves never learned the ballads. Often it is the children who teach the songs to their parents, piecing together a memory that had begun to fade.

Winning international fame, however, was never what Camake had in mind when he started the group. __34__

After Typhoon Morakot struck in August 2009, Taiwu Village and its school had to move down from the mountains. Camake said, “We could not take the forest or our houses with us, but we were able to bring our culture along.” He promised to keep singing with the children for as long as they were willing to sing.

passage.title: 研究快樂這件事（The Science of Happiness）
passage.text:
Not long ago, joy wasn’t considered serious enough for psychologists to study. These scientists traditionally helped people with depression or other mental illnesses, not those who were already doing well. But today, happiness is a hot subject of research. __31__

However, this kind of research faces significant obstacles. For one thing, it is difficult to measure a feeling like happiness scientifically. Suppose your best friend says she feels great but is crying a lot and acting more depressed than usual. For the purposes of a scientific study, would you rate her as happy or sad? __32__ On a scale of 1 to 10, how can we be sure that my “8” is happier than your “6”?

In recent years, however, researchers have found better ways to measure happiness. __33__ Real smiles usually look quite different from the forced ones people put on for photographs. A real smile tends to reach the eyes and make the skin around them crinkle, while a fake one often moves only the mouth.

__34__ Other research-backed happiness boosters include keeping a diary of your future dreams, setting and pursuing goals, making friends and family members a big part of your life, expressing optimism about your future, extending gratitude to people who help you, and exercising regularly. The good news is that most of these habits cost little or nothing, so almost anyone can start practicing them today.

passage.title: 卡內基：從送信童到慈善家（Andrew Carnegie: From Messenger Boy to Philanthropist）
passage.text:
Andrew Carnegie, one of the richest men of his time, was born in 1835 to a weaver’s family in Scotland. As a child, he was expected to follow his father’s trade. But when factory machines put hand weavers like his father out of work, the family had to leave for a new life in America.

In 1848, the Carnegies settled near Pittsburgh, then a busy industrial city. Andrew went to work at once, first in a cotton factory and later as a messenger boy in a telegraph office. __31__ When he delivered messages to the city theater, he often stayed to watch plays, especially Shakespeare’s. On Saturday nights, he borrowed books from a small library that a generous local man had opened to working boys.

__32__ Many railroad bridges were still made of wood, which could easily catch fire. He started a company to replace them with stronger iron bridges, and it made him rich. Later, he turned to steel, using a new method from Britain to make it cheaply and in large amounts. By 1900, his mills alone produced more steel than all of Great Britain.

However, Carnegie often said he felt uneasy about the life of a businessman. In a note to himself in 1868, he warned that a life spent chasing more and more money would harm him beyond repair. He wished instead to spend more time studying and reading widely. __33__

For the rest of his life, Carnegie devoted himself to giving away his fortune. He believed that a man who dies rich “dies disgraced.” __34__ Remembering the small library of his boyhood, he paid to build more than 2,500 libraries around the world. By the time he died in 1919, he had given away about $350 million.

passage.title: 非洲學校走向數位化（Schools in Africa Going Digital）
passage.text:
Grace Wambui, a 14-year-old pupil in Nairobi, had never touched a tablet computer. But when tablets arrived at Amaf School in Kawangware, a low-income area of the Kenyan capital, it took her only about a minute to work out how to use one. Lessons there used to rely on a blackboard and a handful of worn-out textbooks. Now children in groups of five take turns swiping the touch screens of tablets loaded with a multimedia version of Kenya’s school curriculum.

The tablets at Amaf School are part of a pilot project run by eLimu, a Kenyan technology start-up. Many firms are betting on a boom in digital education in Kenya and elsewhere in Africa. Some business leaders even expect it to take off like M-Pesa, the hugely successful service that lets Kenyans send money by mobile phone. __31__

Such a change would come at just the right time for Kenya’s schools. When Kenya made primary education free in 2003, about 1.3 million extra pupils poured into its classrooms. __32__ At many schools, class sizes soared, some doubling almost overnight. Books, desks, and even pencils ran short.

__33__ Amazon has reported that sales of its Kindle e-readers in Africa grew tenfold in a single year. Intel has been helping African governments buy low-cost computers. In Nigeria, the firm brought together a local publisher and a mobile phone company to offer exam-preparation tools by phone, a service that soon became very popular.

__34__ The early signs suggest that they do. In Ghana, children who were given e-readers by a charity made measurable gains in reading. In Ethiopia, children with no teachers worked out on their own how to use tablets and learned the English alphabet. At Amaf School, average marks in science rose from 58 to 73 in a single term.

passage.title: 斯巴達松超級馬拉松的魅力（The Allure of the Spartathlon Ultra-Marathon）
passage.text:
In the Spartathlon, one of the world’s toughest ultra-marathons, runners cover 246 kilometers, almost six marathons, within 36 hours. The runners start in Athens and run all the way to the historic city of Sparta.

The race’s roots go back to 490 B.C., when an Athenian named Pheidippides made the journey to Sparta to ask the Spartans for help against the invading Persians. __31__ In 1982, this story sparked the interest of John Foden, a British air-force officer and long-distance runner, who wondered if anyone could really cover that distance so quickly. Foden and four other runners from the air force decided to see for themselves. Three of the five made it to Sparti, as the town is now called, in less than 40 hours. Their success led to the first Spartathlon a year later.

__32__ The Spartathlon is not the hardest race in the world, but it combines many different tests. There is the heat of the Greek day, and then the sharp drop in temperature when darkness falls. There are long climbs, and in the middle of the night, runners must cross a mountain about 1,200 meters high. Above all, there is the constant pressure of the clock. __33__

As finishers receive a wreath and water from schoolgirls, many are overjoyed. However, the joy does not last long. __34__ After the race, Sparti looks like the set of a zombie movie, as runners move slowly and painfully around the town. But the urge to do it all over again soon appears.

passage.title: 麝香貓咖啡的價格與來歷（The Price and Origin of Kopi Luwak）
passage.text:
Coffee experts are willing to pay large sums of money for high-quality beans. Premium varieties such as Kona and Blue Mountain are known to cost far more than ordinary coffee. Then there is Kopi Luwak (translated as “civet coffee”), one of the most expensive coffees in the world, which can sell for as much as US$80 a cup.

Its high price is easy to understand, since genuine Kopi Luwak is produced only in very small amounts. __31__ The coffee plants themselves are not rare; the beans found in civet droppings are. That’s right—beans picked out of the body waste of the palm civet. Coffee beans do not become Kopi Luwak until they have passed through the animal’s body.

__32__ Found in South and Southeast Asia, it comes out at night and often visits coffee farms to feed on the cherries. It swallows them whole but digests only their soft outer flesh. Farmers then pick the hard beans out of its droppings, wash them, and roast them.

While the beans survive the trip through the animal, they do not come out unchanged. Juices in the civet’s digestive system break down some of the proteins in the beans, which is believed to make the coffee less bitter. Digestion may not be the whole story, however. __33__

Kopi Luwak is said to taste unlike any other coffee, with hints of caramel and an earthy flavor. Its popularity, though, has come at a high price for the civets. __34__ Fed almost nothing but coffee cherries and kept on wire floors, some of them grow thin and develop painful sores. Since they cannot choose their own cherries, the coffee they produce is often of poorer quality, too.

passage.title: 馬雅城市為什麼消失（Why the Mayan Cities Vanished）
passage.text:
The Maya built a remarkable civilization that covered much of what is now southern Mexico and northern Central America. __31__ Mayan culture took shape in the Preclassic Period, but it reached its highest development in the Classic Period, from about 250 to 900 AD. During this time, Mayan society was one of the most densely populated and culturally active in the world.

Rather than a single empire, Mayan civilization was made up of many separate city-states that shared a common culture. Strangely, after the Classic Period ended, many of these cities ceased to be centers of importance. __32__ Only the cities were lost, swallowed up by the tropical jungle. Not until the last two hundred years or so did travelers and scholars rediscover and study them. One question that interests scholars is why these cities simply disappeared.

__33__ Toward the end of the Classic Period, there was large-scale, continuous warfare among the city-states. The rulers were highly competitive and made fierce war on one another. Overpopulation was probably also to blame. The Mayan population reached as many as 200 people per square kilometer, among the highest densities in the pre-industrial world. __34__

Studies of ancient pollen show that in many areas, very few trees were left. The loss of so many trees damaged the local environment and helped cause a lack of water and, in time, drought. Thus warfare, overpopulation, overuse of resources, and destruction of the environment all appear to be factors in the disappearance of the Mayan cities.
